definition:
Election is God's free choosing. In Scripture God chooses persons for tasks (Abraham, Aaron and the Levites, David, the prophets, the apostles), a people to be his own (Israel, and in the New Testament the church drawn from every nation), a place where his name will dwell (Jerusalem), and above all one person, the Servant and Messiah whom the Father calls “My Chosen One” (Isaiah 42:1). The New Testament also speaks of believers as chosen “in Him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4) for salvation and holiness. Two features run through every kind of election in the Bible. It rests on God's love and purpose rather than on the merit of the chosen (Deuteronomy 7:7-8; Romans 9:11), and it is always for something: the chosen are chosen to be a blessing, to bear fruit, to be holy, to proclaim God's praises. Calling is the act by which God summons the chosen: Abram is called out of Ur, Israel out of Egypt, disciples from their nets, and believers “out of darkness into His marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9). How God's choosing relates to human faith is one of the church's longest debates, treated at length at /theology/doctrine/sovereignty-and-freedom and /theology/doctrine/soteriology; this study traces what the Bible says and how the church has read it.

The main Hebrew verb is bachar, ‘to choose’, used of God choosing Israel, the tribe of Levi, David, and Zion, and of human beings choosing what they will serve. The related noun bachir means ‘chosen one’ (Psalm 89:3; Isaiah 42:1). Sometimes the Bible uses yada', ‘to know’, for God's choosing: the BSB renders it “I have chosen him” in Genesis 18:19, and in Amos 3:2 God says, “Only you have I known from all the families of the earth.” God's ‘treasured possession’ is segullah (Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6). In Greek the verb is eklegomai, ‘to choose’; the adjective eklektos, ‘chosen’ or ‘elect’; and the noun eklogē, ‘choice’ or ‘election’ (Romans 9:11; 11:5; 1 Thessalonians 1:4). Proorizō, ‘to decide beforehand’ or ‘predestine’, appears six times (Acts 4:28; Romans 8:29-30; 1 Corinthians 2:7; Ephesians 1:5, 11). Proginōskō and prognōsis, ‘to know beforehand’ and ‘foreknowledge’, raise a central interpretive question: some take them to mean God's foresight of who would believe, others, noting the Hebrew use of ‘know’ for choosing and 1 Peter 1:20, where Christ himself was “known before the foundation of the world”, take them to mean God's prior, loving commitment to persons. The calling words are kaleō, ‘to call’, klēsis, ‘calling’, and klētos, ‘called’. Jesus uses ‘called’ for the wide invitation, “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 22:14), while Paul often uses it for the summons that brings a person to faith (Romans 8:30; 1 Corinthians 1:24).
ot:
Election begins with Abraham. God calls him out of his country and promises, “I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you,” adding, “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:2-3). From the first, the one is chosen for the sake of the many. Later God says, “I have chosen him, so that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just” (Genesis 18:19); election creates a way of life, not only a privilege. Genesis then traces a line of promise through a series of surprising choices: Isaac rather than Ishmael (Genesis 17:21), Jacob rather than Esau, announced before the twins were born, “the older will serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23), and later Joseph and Judah rather than Reuben. The pattern of the younger preferred over the older recurs so often that it becomes a signature of God's freedom. The ones passed over are not cursed: God promises to bless Ishmael and make him “a great nation” (Genesis 17:20), and Esau is reconciled with his brother (Genesis 33).

At Sinai God tells Israel, “you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations,” for “the whole earth is Mine,” and “you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:5-6). A priest stands between God and others, so the title gives Israel a vocation toward the nations. Deuteronomy explains the choice in the plainest terms the Old Testament offers. “The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples, for you were the fewest of all peoples. But because the LORD loved you and kept the oath He swore to your fathers” (Deuteronomy 7:7-8). Nor was it for Israel's goodness: “it is not because of your righteousness that the LORD your God is giving you this good land to possess, for you are a stiff-necked people” (Deuteronomy 9:6). The ground of election is love that has no reason outside itself, and the God who chooses owns “the heavens, even the highest heavens, and the earth and everything in it” (Deuteronomy 10:14). Deuteronomy also speaks of God choosing a place for his name (Deuteronomy 12:5), the tribe of Levi for priestly service (Deuteronomy 18:5), and the king (Deuteronomy 17:15).

The history books show that election to an office can be lost while God's larger purpose holds. Samuel presents Saul as “the one the LORD has chosen” (1 Samuel 10:24), yet after his disobedience God rejects him as king (1 Samuel 15:26). God then passes over Jesse's older sons, telling Samuel that “man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7), and chooses the youngest, who is out with the sheep. The Psalms celebrate the choice: God “chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which He loved,” and “chose David His servant and took him from the sheepfolds” (Psalm 78:68, 70). The prophets refused to let election become national pride. Amos turns it into accountability: “Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (Amos 3:2). He even reminds Israel that God brought other peoples from their homelands too (Amos 9:7). As judgment falls, the theme of the remnant appears. God tells Elijah, “I have reserved seven thousand in Israel” who have not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:18), and Isaiah announces that “A remnant will return” (Isaiah 10:21). Within the chosen people, God preserves a faithful people.

In exile the promise is renewed. Isaiah speaks to a defeated Israel: “I have chosen and not rejected you” (Isaiah 41:9), and names Israel God's chosen servant and witness (Isaiah 43:10; 44:1-2). God even calls the Persian king Cyrus by name “For the sake of Jacob My servant and Israel My chosen one” (Isaiah 45:4). Then the Servant appears as an individual: “Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will bring justice to the nations” (Isaiah 42:1). God will make this Servant “a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). The Chosen One gathers up Israel's calling and carries it to the world. After the return, Haggai tells Zerubbabel, a descendant of David, “I have chosen you” (Haggai 2:23), keeping the royal hope alive, and Malachi answers a doubting people with God's covenant love: “Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated” (Malachi 1:2-3). In its context the saying concerns the nations of Israel and Edom, and the language of love and hate is the language of covenant choice, a way of saying which one God bound himself to, not a description of emotion. In the centuries before Jesus, Jewish writings kept the theme alive: the Qumran community spoke of itself as God's elect, and the Similitudes of Enoch (1 Enoch 37 to 71) call a coming heavenly figure ‘the Elect One’.
nt:
The New Testament begins its account of election with Jesus himself. At the transfiguration the Father's voice says, “This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!” (Luke 9:35), where the Greek is eklelegmenos, ‘chosen’; many later manuscripts read ‘beloved’ instead, echoing Mark and Matthew, and modern editions follow the older witnesses. At the cross the rulers mock him as “the Christ of God, the Chosen One” (Luke 23:35), and Peter calls him the living stone “rejected by men but chosen and precious in God's sight” (1 Peter 2:4), quoting Isaiah 28:16. Jesus chooses the Twelve after a night of prayer (Luke 6:13), and his choice of them is for mission: “You did not choose Me, but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit” (John 15:16). That this choosing was to an office rather than a guarantee of salvation is clear from Judas: “Have I not chosen you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil!” (John 6:70). Jesus speaks of “the elect” for whose sake days of distress will be shortened and whom the angels will gather (Matthew 24:22, 31), of those the Father has given him who will come to him (John 6:37; 17:6), and of the kingdom “prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). His parable of the wedding feast ends, “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 22:14): the invitation goes out widely, and those who refuse it or come on their own terms are excluded.

In Acts, the risen Lord calls Saul of Tarsus “My chosen instrument to carry My name before the Gentiles” (Acts 9:15), and James sees in the conversion of Gentiles God's purpose “to take from them a people to be His own” (Acts 15:14). Election here serves the spread of the gospel; the Lord tells Paul in Corinth to keep speaking, “because I have many people in this city” (Acts 18:10). Paul's letters give the fullest teaching. In Romans 8 he sets election at the head of a chain of God's acts: “those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son,” and “those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified” (Romans 8:29-30). The goal is likeness to Christ, and the point is assurance: “Who will bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33).

Romans 9 to 11 answers a painful question: if Jesus is Israel's Messiah, why have most of Israel not believed, and has God's word failed? Paul answers that “not all who are descended from Israel are Israel” (Romans 9:6) and that God's choice of Jacob over Esau was made “before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, in order that God's plan of election might stand, not by works but by Him who calls” (Romans 9:11-12). At the present time “there is a remnant chosen by grace,” and “if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works” (Romans 11:5-6). Yet Paul insists that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1), that regarding election they “are loved on account of the patriarchs,” for “God's gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:28-29), and that “God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone” (Romans 11:32). He warns Gentile believers not to boast over the broken branches (Romans 11:18). The section ends not with a solution but with praise: “How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways” (Romans 11:33). Interpreters differ on whether Romans 9 speaks chiefly of individuals chosen for salvation (the reading of Augustine, Calvin, and recent writers such as Thomas Schreiner and John Piper) or of peoples and their roles in God's plan (the reading of many Arminian and some other interpreters), and many hold that it involves both.

Ephesians opens with a long blessing: God “chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence,” and “predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 1:4-5), all “to the praise of His glorious grace” (Ephesians 1:6). The phrase ‘in Him’ recurs throughout the passage, and the believers were sealed with the Spirit when they “heard and believed” the gospel (Ephesians 1:13). Election appears as a cause for humility and a call to holy living: God “chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong” so “that no one may boast in His presence” (1 Corinthians 1:27, 29); the elect are to clothe themselves “with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience” (Colossians 3:12); God has “chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith” (James 2:5). Paul recognizes the Thessalonians' election by the gospel's power among them (1 Thessalonians 1:4-5) and says God chose them “to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth,” calling them “through our gospel” (2 Thessalonians 2:13-14); some manuscripts read ‘as firstfruits’ instead of ‘from the beginning’ in that verse. The means belong to the plan. Paul endures suffering “for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation” (2 Timothy 2:10), and he could wish himself cursed for the sake of his unbelieving kin (Romans 9:3).

Peter writes to “the elect who are exiles,” chosen “according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:1-2), a Trinitarian account of election aimed at obedience. He applies Israel's titles from Exodus 19 to scattered churches of Jews and Gentiles: “you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation,” chosen “to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you” (1 Peter 2:9). Second Peter urges believers to “make your calling and election sure” (2 Peter 1:10) by growing in faith, virtue, and love. Revelation speaks of names written in the Lamb's book of life “from the foundation of the world” (Revelation 17:8; compare 13:8, where the Greek could attach that phrase either to the writing of the names or to the Lamb who was slain), and it describes those with the Lamb as “His called and chosen and faithful ones” (Revelation 17:14).

keyTexts.why: God calls Abram and promises that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him. Election is for the blessing of others from the very start.
Before the twins are born, God says the older will serve the younger. Paul cites it as proof that election rests on God's call, not human works.
God chose Israel not for its size but because he loved them and kept his oath. The Old Testament's clearest statement of the ground of election.
God passes over Jesse's older sons and chooses David, for the LORD sees the heart. The pattern of God choosing the overlooked.
God presents his Servant, his Chosen One, who will bring justice to the nations. The New Testament applies this title to Jesus.
Because God has known Israel alone among the nations, he will hold them to account. Election brings responsibility, not immunity.
Jesus chose his disciples and appointed them to bear lasting fruit. Election is God's initiative and aims at mission.
Those God foreknew he predestined, called, justified, and glorified, and no charge can stand against his elect. Election grounds assurance.
God's plan of election stands not by works but by him who calls, and his mercy does not depend on human desire or effort. The most debated passage on the doctrine.
God has not rejected his people; a remnant is chosen by grace. Election is by grace and not by works.
Israel is still beloved for the patriarchs' sake, God's call is irrevocable, and Paul ends in worship. Election kept within mercy and mystery.
God chose the foolish, weak, and lowly so that no one may boast. Election rules out pride.
God chose believers in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and adopted, to the praise of his grace. The fullest statement of election in Christ.
God chose believers to be saved through the Spirit's sanctifying work and faith in the truth, calling them through the gospel. The means belong to the plan.
Christ is the chosen stone, and the church is a chosen people and royal priesthood called to proclaim God's praises. Israel's calling applied to the church.

history:
The earliest Christian writers spoke of election mainly to insist that salvation is God's gift and that human beings are still responsible, against pagan fate and against Gnostic teachers who divided humanity into fixed natures. Many Greek fathers, John Chrysostom among them in his homilies on Romans, explained God's choosing by his foreknowledge of how people would respond. Augustine of Hippo changed the course of Western theology. In his early exposition of Romans (about 394) he explained election by God's foresight of faith, but in his reply To Simplician (about 396) he concluded that faith itself is God's gift, so that election cannot rest on it. His late works On the Predestination of the Saints and On the Gift of Perseverance (428 to 429) taught that God chooses some, out of fallen humanity, freely and unconditionally, and gives them faith and perseverance. The Second Council of Orange (529) affirmed that the beginning of faith is a gift of grace and condemned anyone who says God predestines people to evil, without adopting all of Augustine's teaching on predestination. In the ninth century the monk Gottschalk of Orbais taught a strict double predestination, to life and to death, and was condemned at synods at Mainz (848) and Quierzy (849). Thomas Aquinas, in the Summa Theologiae (first part, question 23), treated predestination as part of providence and taught that it is not caused by foreseen merits, while reprobation consists in God permitting some to fall.

The Reformers made election a doctrine of comfort. Martin Luther's The Bondage of the Will (1525) grounded salvation entirely in God's will. John Calvin, in the Institutes (Book 3, chapters 21 to 24, final edition 1559) and in Concerning the Eternal Predestination of God (1552), taught that God chooses some for salvation and passes over others, and urged that the doctrine be approached with humility and looked for in Christ. The Lutheran Formula of Concord (1577, article 11) taught that election is the cause of the salvation of the elect but that God has not decreed anyone's damnation, which comes from human unbelief, and it counselled believers to seek their election in Christ and the gospel rather than in God's hidden counsel. The Council of Trent (session 6, 1547) warned that no one should presume to know with certainty, apart from special revelation, that they are among the predestined. The followers of Jacobus Arminius set out five articles in the Remonstrance of 1610, the first teaching that God elects those whom he foresees will believe and persevere. The Synod of Dort (1618 to 1619) answered with the Canons of Dort, teaching unconditional election; the Canons are usually read as infralapsarian in shape (God's choosing considers humanity as already fallen), though the synod did not condemn the supralapsarian view associated with Theodore Beza. The Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 3) and the Particular Baptists' Second London Confession (1689) followed Dort, while General Baptists and later Methodists followed the Arminian account.

The debate continued in every tradition. John Wesley preached against unconditional election in his sermon Free Grace (1739), and George Whitefield answered him in a public letter (1740). Andrew Fuller's The Gospel Worthy of All Acceptation (1785) defended the free offer of the gospel to all against hyper-Calvinist hesitation, and helped launch the modern Baptist missionary movement. In the Roman Catholic Church, Pope Innocent X condemned five propositions of Jansenism in 1653, and the Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992, paragraph 600) teaches that God's eternal plan of predestination includes each person's free response to his grace. The Eastern Orthodox Synod of Jerusalem (1672), in the Confession of Dositheus, taught that God predestined to glory those he foresaw would rightly use their free will, and rejected unconditional reprobation.

In the twentieth century Karl Barth, in Church Dogmatics II/2 (1942), reframed the doctrine around Jesus Christ as both the electing God and the elected human being, who takes on himself the rejection that belongs to sinners. Lesslie Newbigin, in The Gospel in a Pluralist Society (1989), recovered the Bible's emphasis that God chooses some to be bearers of his salvation for the sake of all. Robert Shank's Elect in the Son (1970) and William Klein's The New Chosen People (1990) argued for a corporate election of the church in Christ, while John Piper's The Justification of God (1983) and Thomas Schreiner's work on Romans defended individual unconditional election. N. T. Wright has stressed Israel's election as a vocation to bring God's blessing to the world, fulfilled in the Messiah.

differ.body: Before creation God freely chose particular persons out of fallen humanity for salvation, not because he foresaw their faith or merit but out of sheer grace, and he gives them the faith by which they believe. Defenders from Augustine and Thomas Aquinas to John Calvin, the Canons of Dort, the Westminster Confession, and writers such as John Piper and Thomas Schreiner point to Romans 9:11-16, Ephesians 1:4-5, John 6:37-44, and Acts 13:48. They argue that if election rested on foreseen faith, the final difference between the saved and the lost would lie in the creature, and grace would no longer be grace (Romans 11:6). Within this view, supralapsarians and infralapsarians differ on the logical order of God's decrees. They hold that the doctrine humbles pride, grounds assurance, and gives confidence in evangelism, since God has a people who will hear.

God chose to save all who believe in Christ, and he elects individuals as he foreknows their faith, which his prevenient grace makes possible for everyone but does not force. Defenders from Jacobus Arminius and John Wesley to Thomas Oden, Roger Olson, and Jerry Walls, with many Eastern Orthodox teachers and some Baptist Traditionalists, point to 1 Peter 1:2 and Romans 8:29, where election follows foreknowledge, to God's desire that all be saved (1 Timothy 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9), and to the sincere universal invitations of the gospel. They argue that unconditional election cannot be reconciled with God's love for every person or with the genuine responsibility of those who refuse him, and that foreknowledge does not cause faith any more than knowing an event causes it.

God's election is first of all the choice of a people, as Israel was chosen in Abraham, and individuals share in it by being united to Christ, the Chosen One, through faith. Defenders such as Robert Shank, William Klein, and Brian Abasciano, drawing on the Old Testament pattern of corporate choosing, point to the repeated ‘in Him’ of Ephesians 1, to Paul's concern in Romans 9 to 11 with Israel and the Gentiles as peoples, and to 1 Peter 2:9, where the church as a whole is a chosen people. They argue that this reading follows the Bible's own categories more closely than debates about individual decrees, and that it keeps election tied to Christ and to mission. Many who hold it are Arminian; some Reformed writers also stress the corporate dimension while keeping individual election.

God has elected his own to salvation in Christ, and that election is the sole cause of their salvation, but God has not predestined anyone to damnation; those who are lost perish by their own unbelief. The Formula of Concord (1577, article 11) holds both truths without attempting to reconcile them, and teaches that election is to be sought in Christ, in the gospel, and in the sacraments rather than in speculation about God's hidden will. Lutheran theologians argue that this is exactly what Scripture teaches, God's grace alone saving and human guilt alone condemning, and that any system which explains the difference between the saved and the lost goes beyond what God has revealed.

differ.view: Christ as the elect one (Barth and his heirs)
differ.body: Karl Barth, in Church Dogmatics II/2 (1942), argued that the doctrine of election must begin with Jesus Christ, who is both the electing God and the elected human being. In him God chose humanity for fellowship with himself and chose for himself the rejection that sinners deserve, which he bore at the cross. Defenders read Ephesians 1:4 and 1 Peter 1:20 as placing Christ at the center of God's eternal choosing, and they argue that this turns election from a source of fear into good news. Critics from several traditions ask whether it leads to universal salvation, which Barth himself neither affirmed nor ruled out.

errors:
The church has rejected accounts of election that ground it in human merit. Pelagianism, condemned in 418 and 431, and the teachings later called semi-Pelagian, answered at Orange in 529, made the first move toward God a human achievement; every tradition since confesses that salvation begins with grace. The church has also rejected the teaching that God predestines people to sin, which Orange condemned, and fatalism, which treats election as an impersonal decree that makes prayer, preaching, and repentance pointless. Hyper-Calvinism, which hesitates to offer the gospel freely to all or to call all people to repent, has been rejected by mainstream Reformed churches as well as by every other tradition, since the apostles preached to everyone and commanded all to repent.

Other distortions are moral. Election has been twisted into pride, national or personal, as if the chosen were better than others; Moses forbade it (Deuteronomy 9:4-6), Amos denounced it, John the Baptist warned that “God can raise up children for Abraham” from stones (Matthew 3:9), and Paul told Gentile believers, “do not boast over those branches” (Romans 11:18). The church's long history of contempt for the Jewish people stands under that warning. Election has also been used as license, as though the chosen could live as they please; Scripture says they were chosen “to be holy and blameless” (Ephesians 1:4). And it has been turned into anxious self-examination, people searching their feelings for proof that they are among the elect. The Formula of Concord and the Canons of Dort (first head, article 16) both counsel such people to look to Christ and to use the means of grace rather than to peer into God's hidden counsel.
life:
Election tells believers that their standing with God began in his love, not in their achievement, so it cannot be ended by their failure to earn it. That is why the New Testament uses the doctrine to comfort the persecuted (Romans 8:33), to strengthen the scattered (1 Peter 1:1), and to steady the fearful. It also removes every ground for boasting, since the chosen were often the youngest, the weakest, and the least likely. People who were once “not a people” have been made “the people of God” (1 Peter 2:10), and that identity does not depend on ancestry, status, or success.

Election is also a summons. Abraham was chosen so that the nations would be blessed, Israel to be a kingdom of priests, the disciples to bear fruit, the church to proclaim God's praises. A person who knows they have been chosen by grace is sent to others with the same grace, and Paul's own example shows that belief in election drove him to preach, to suffer for others, and to pray for those who had not believed. Christians who disagree about how election works can agree on this: the chosen are chosen for the sake of the world, and their calling is to live as those who have received mercy.
questions: Deuteronomy 7 says God chose Israel because he loved them, not because they were many or good. What does it mean for you that God's choosing rests on his love rather than on your qualities?
From Abraham to the church, the chosen are always chosen for the sake of others. How does that change the way you think about being one of God's people?

Romans 9 to 11 moves from hard questions about God's choosing to worship. Why do you think Paul ends there, and what does that suggest about how Christians should hold their disagreements about election?
